# Overview

This computational report documents the preparation, statistical analysis,
model evaluation, NIST-aligned architecture assessment, and financial
sensitivity analysis of the HHS HIPAA breach dataset.

The analysis examines patterns among reported healthcare breaches and evaluates
observable characteristics associated with severe breaches. A severe breach is
defined as one affecting at least 100,000 individuals.

To keep the HTML report readable, the main page displays the tables needed to
interpret the findings and decisions. Detailed data-quality checks,
intermediate model diagnostics, component rankings, and complete sensitivity
tables are still calculated and exported in the reproducibility bundle.

::: {.callout-note}
## Reporting Period

The dataset includes records through 2026. Because 2026 is incomplete, trend
figures based on complete calendar years are reported through 2025.
:::

# Data Preparation

## Import and Standardization

The original worksheet is preserved as `raw_data`, while a separate copy is
used for analysis. Date and breach-size fields are standardized before the
analytic sample is constructed.

```{python}
#| label: setup-data
#| echo: true

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
from pathlib import Path

sns.set_theme(
    style="whitegrid",
    context="notebook",
)

REPORT_COLORS = {
    "blue": "#2F6B8A",
    "teal": "#2A7F7F",
    "gold": "#C9972B",
    "red": "#B44C43",
    "gray": "#6B7280",
}

def format_p_value(value):
    """Format p-values consistently for publication tables."""
    return "<0.0001" if float(value) < 0.0001 else f"{float(value):.4f}"

data_candidates = [
    Path("../data/hhs_hipaa_breach_modeling_data_2009_2026.csv"),
    Path("HHS_HIPAA_Breach_Modeling_Dataset_2009-2026.xlsx"),
    *sorted(Path(".").glob("HHS_HIPAA_Breach_Modeling_Dataset_2009-2026*.xlsx")),
]

file_path = next(
    (candidate for candidate in data_candidates if candidate.exists()),
    None,
)

if file_path is None:
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        "Add the repository CSV under ../data or place the modeling workbook beside this Quarto file."
    )

if file_path.suffix.lower() == ".csv":
    raw_data = pd.read_csv(file_path)
else:
    raw_data = pd.read_excel(
        file_path,
        sheet_name="Modeling_Data",
    )

data = raw_data.drop(
    columns=["Unnamed: 0"],
    errors="ignore",
).copy()

data["Submission_Date"] = pd.to_datetime(
    data["Submission_Date"],
    errors="coerce",
)

data["Individuals_Affected"] = pd.to_numeric(
    data["Individuals_Affected"],
    errors="coerce",
)
```

## Analytic Sample

The analytic sample is restricted to records identified as model-ready in the
prepared dataset.

```{python}
#| label: cell-analytic-sample
#| echo: false

analysis_data = data.loc[
    data["Model_Ready_Flag"].eq(1)
].copy()

print(f"Analytic sample size: {len(analysis_data):,}")
```

## Severe-Breach Outcome

A severe breach is defined as a reported breach affecting at least 100,000
individuals.

$$
Y_i =
\begin{cases}
1, & A_i \geq 100{,}000 \\
0, & A_i < 100{,}000
\end{cases}
$$

where \(A_i\) represents the number of individuals affected by reported breach
\(i\).

The severe-breach indicator is independently recalculated from
`Individuals_Affected` and compared with the existing outcome field as a data
validation check.

```{python}
#| label: validate-severe-outcome
#| echo: false

analysis_data["Severe_Breach_Check"] = np.where(
    analysis_data["Individuals_Affected"].notna(),
    analysis_data["Individuals_Affected"].ge(100_000).astype(int),
    np.nan,
)

valid_outcomes = analysis_data.dropna(
    subset=["Large_Breach_100K", "Severe_Breach_Check"]
)

outcome_mismatch_count = (
    valid_outcomes["Large_Breach_100K"]
    .ne(valid_outcomes["Severe_Breach_Check"])
    .sum()
)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-severe-breach-outcome
#| tbl-cap: "Distribution of the severe-breach outcome"
#| echo: false

outcome_counts = (
    analysis_data["Large_Breach_100K"]
    .value_counts()
    .reindex([0, 1], fill_value=0)
)

known_outcomes = outcome_counts.sum()

outcome_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Outcome": [
        "Non-severe breach",
        "Severe breach",
        "Total known outcomes",
    ],
    "N": [
        outcome_counts[0],
        outcome_counts[1],
        known_outcomes,
    ],
    "Percent": [
        outcome_counts[0] / known_outcomes * 100,
        outcome_counts[1] / known_outcomes * 100,
        100.0,
    ],
})

outcome_summary["Percent"] = outcome_summary["Percent"].round(2)

display(
    outcome_summary.style
    .format({"N": "{:,.0f}", "Percent": "{:.2f}%"})
    .hide(axis="index")
)
print(f"Outcome validation mismatches: {outcome_mismatch_count:,}")
```

Severe breaches represent a minority of the analytic sample, indicating a
substantially imbalanced binary outcome.

# Descriptive Analysis

## Individuals Affected

Because breach size is strongly right-skewed, the descriptive summary emphasizes
the median, interquartile range, and upper percentiles in addition to the mean.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-affected-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive statistics for individuals affected"
#| echo: false

affected = analysis_data["Individuals_Affected"].dropna()

q1 = affected.quantile(0.25)
q3 = affected.quantile(0.75)

affected_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Statistic": [
        "Count",
        "Mean",
        "Standard Deviation",
        "Minimum",
        "25th Percentile",
        "Median",
        "75th Percentile",
        "IQR",
        "95th Percentile",
        "99th Percentile",
        "Maximum",
    ],
    "Value": [
        affected.count(),
        affected.mean(),
        affected.std(),
        affected.min(),
        q1,
        affected.median(),
        q3,
        q3 - q1,
        affected.quantile(0.95),
        affected.quantile(0.99),
        affected.max(),

})

affected_summary["Value"] = affected_summary["Value"].round(2)

display(
    affected_summary.style
    .format({"Value": "{:,.0f}"})
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

## Distribution of Breach Size

The distribution of individuals affected is examined using both the raw scale
through the 99th percentile and a log-transformed scale that retains the full
range of reported breach sizes.

```{python}
#| label: fig-breach-size-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of individuals affected by reported healthcare breaches"
#| fig-alt: "Two-panel breach-size distribution showing a strongly right-skewed raw scale and a more readable logarithmic scale."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false

upper_99 = affected.quantile(0.99)
raw_plot_data = affected.loc[affected <= upper_99]
log_affected = np.log1p(affected)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))

axes[0].hist(raw_plot_data, bins=50, edgecolor="black")
axes[0].set_title("Breach Size Through the 99th Percentile")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Individuals Affected")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Number of Breaches")

axes[1].hist(log_affected, bins=50, edgecolor="black")
axes[1].set_title("Log-Transformed Breach Size")
axes[1].set_xlabel("log(1 + Individuals Affected)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Number of Breaches")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

As shown in @fig-breach-size-distribution, breach size is strongly right-skewed,
with a relatively small number of breaches affecting substantially larger
populations.

## Categorical Descriptive Analysis

Categorical summaries describe the distribution of breach type, covered entity
type, information location, and business-associate involvement.

```{python}
#| label: categorical-summary
#| echo: false
#| output: false

categorical_variables = [
    "Breach_Type",
    "Covered_Entity_Type",
    "Information_Location",
    "Business_Associate_Present",
]


def frequency_table(frame, variable):
    """Return counts and percentages for one categorical variable."""

    values = (
        frame[variable]
        .fillna("Unknown")
        .astype(str)
        .str.strip()
    )

    result = (
        values.value_counts()
        .rename_axis(variable)
        .reset_index(name="Breaches")
    )

    result["Percent"] = (
        result["Breaches"] / len(frame) * 100
    ).round(2)

    return result


for variable in categorical_variables:
    print(f"\n{variable}")
    display(frequency_table(analysis_data, variable))
```

## Severe-Breach Rates by Category

Severe-breach rates are calculated within each category using records with known
outcome status.

```{python}
#| label: severe-rate-categories
#| echo: false
#| output: false

def severe_rate_table(frame, variable):
    """Return breach counts and severe-breach rates by category."""

    grouped = frame.copy()

    grouped[variable] = (
        grouped[variable]
        .fillna("Unknown")
        .astype(str)
        .str.strip()
    )

    result = (
        grouped
        .groupby(variable, as_index=False)
        .agg(
            Breaches=("Record_ID", "count"),
            Known_Outcomes=("Large_Breach_100K", "count"),
            Severe_Breaches=("Large_Breach_100K", "sum"),
        )
    )

    result["Severe_Rate"] = np.where(
        result["Known_Outcomes"] > 0,
        result["Severe_Breaches"] / result["Known_Outcomes"] * 100,
        np.nan,
    )

    return result.round({"Severe_Rate": 2})


for variable in categorical_variables:
    print(f"\nSevere-breach rates by {variable}")
    display(severe_rate_table(analysis_data, variable))
```

# Statistical Analysis

## Binary Indicators and Confidence Intervals

Binary indicators are created for selected breach types, information locations,
and business-associate involvement. Breach-type and information-location
indicators are not mutually exclusive because individual records may contain
multiple classifications.

```{python}
#| label: create-binary-indicators
#| echo: true

from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency, kruskal, mannwhitneyu
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint


def contains_indicator(frame, column, text):
    """Return a binary indicator for whether a text field contains a value."""

    return (
        frame[column]
        .fillna("")
        .astype(str)
        .str.contains(text, case=False, regex=False)
        .astype(int)
    )


indicator_definitions = {
    "Breach_Hacking_IT": ("Breach_Type", "Hacking/IT Incident"),
    "Breach_Unauthorized_Access": (
        "Breach_Type",
        "Unauthorized Access/Disclosure",
    ),
    "Breach_Theft": ("Breach_Type", "Theft"),
    "Breach_Loss": ("Breach_Type", "Loss"),
    "Breach_Improper_Disposal": ("Breach_Type", "Improper Disposal"),
    "Location_Desktop": ("Information_Location", "Desktop Computer"),
    "Location_EMR": ("Information_Location", "Electronic Medical Record"),
    "Location_Laptop": ("Information_Location", "Laptop"),
    "Location_Network_Server": ("Information_Location", "Network Server"),
    "Location_Paper": ("Information_Location", "Paper/Films"),
    "Location_Portable_Device": (
        "Information_Location",
        "Other Portable Electronic Device",
    ),
}

for indicator, (source_column, search_text) in indicator_definitions.items():
    analysis_data[indicator] = contains_indicator(
        analysis_data,
        source_column,
        search_text,
    )

analysis_data["Business_Associate_Yes"] = (
    analysis_data["Business_Associate_Present"]
    .fillna("")
    .astype(str)
    .str.strip()
    .str.lower()
    .eq("yes")
    .astype(int)
)

binary_predictors = [
    *indicator_definitions,
    "Business_Associate_Yes",
]
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-severe-confidence-intervals
#| tbl-cap: "Severe-breach proportions and 95% confidence intervals by binary risk indicator"
#| echo: false

comparison_results = []

for variable in binary_predictors:
    for category in [0, 1]:
        outcome = analysis_data.loc[
            analysis_data[variable].eq(category),
            "Large_Breach_100K",
        ].dropna()

        sample_size = len(outcome)

        if sample_size == 0:
            continue

        severe_count = int(outcome.sum())

        ci_low, ci_high = proportion_confint(
            count=severe_count,
            nobs=sample_size,
            alpha=0.05,
            method="wilson",
        )

        comparison_results.append({
            "Variable": variable,
            "Category": category,
            "N": sample_size,
            "Severe Breaches": severe_count,
            "Severe Rate (%)": severe_count / sample_size * 100,
            "95% CI Lower (%)": ci_low * 100,
            "95% CI Upper (%)": ci_high * 100,
        })

comparison_table = (
    pd.DataFrame(comparison_results)
    .sort_values(["Variable", "Category"])
    .round(2)
)

display(
    comparison_table.style
    .format({
        "N": "{:,.0f}",
        "Severe Breaches": "{:,.0f}",
        "Severe Rate (%)": "{:.2f}%",
        "95% CI Lower (%)": "{:.2f}%",
        "95% CI Upper (%)": "{:.2f}%",
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

## Chi-Square Tests

Chi-square tests evaluate whether severe-breach status is associated with each
binary breach characteristic. Cramér's \(V\) is reported as an effect-size
measure.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-chi-square
#| tbl-cap: "Chi-square tests of association with severe-breach status"
#| echo: false

known_outcomes = analysis_data.dropna(
    subset=["Large_Breach_100K"]
)

chi_square_results = []

for variable in binary_predictors:
    contingency_table = pd.crosstab(
        known_outcomes[variable],
        known_outcomes["Large_Breach_100K"],
    ).reindex(
        index=[0, 1],
        columns=[0, 1],
        fill_value=0,
    )

    chi_square, p_value, degrees_of_freedom, expected = chi2_contingency(
        contingency_table,
        correction=False,
    )

    sample_size = contingency_table.to_numpy().sum()
    # Bias-corrected Cramer's V (Bergsma correction).
    phi_squared = chi_square / sample_size
    rows, columns = contingency_table.shape
    phi_squared_corrected = max(
        0,
        phi_squared
        - ((columns - 1) * (rows - 1)) / (sample_size - 1),
    )
    rows_corrected = rows - ((rows - 1) ** 2) / (sample_size - 1)
    columns_corrected = (
        columns - ((columns - 1) ** 2) / (sample_size - 1)
    )
    denominator = min(rows_corrected - 1, columns_corrected - 1)
    cramers_v = np.sqrt(phi_squared_corrected / denominator)

    chi_square_results.append({
        "Variable": variable,
        "Chi-Square": chi_square,
        "Degrees of Freedom": degrees_of_freedom,
        "P-Value": p_value,
        "Cramer's V": cramers_v,
        "Minimum Expected Count": expected.min(),
    })

chi_square_table = (
    pd.DataFrame(chi_square_results)
    .sort_values("P-Value")
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests

chi_square_table["FDR-Adjusted P-Value"] = multipletests(
    chi_square_table["P-Value"],
    method="fdr_bh",
)[1]

chi_square_table["Significant after FDR Adjustment"] = (
    chi_square_table["FDR-Adjusted P-Value"] < 0.05
).map({True: "Yes", False: "No"})

display(
    chi_square_table.style
    .format({
        "Chi-Square": "{:,.3f}",
        "Degrees of Freedom": "{:,.0f}",
        "P-Value": format_p_value,
        "FDR-Adjusted P-Value": format_p_value,
        "Cramer's V": "{:.3f}",
        "Minimum Expected Count": "{:,.2f}",
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

## Mann–Whitney U Comparisons

Mann–Whitney U tests compare the distribution of individuals affected between
records with and without each binary breach characteristic. The nonparametric
test is used because breach size is strongly right-skewed.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-mann-whitney
#| output: false
#| tbl-cap: "Mann–Whitney U comparisons of breach size by binary risk indicator"
#| echo: false

mann_whitney_results = []

for variable in binary_predictors:
    group_0 = analysis_data.loc[
        analysis_data[variable].eq(0),
        "Individuals_Affected",
    ].dropna()

    group_1 = analysis_data.loc[
        analysis_data[variable].eq(1),
        "Individuals_Affected",
    ].dropna()

    if group_0.empty or group_1.empty:
        continue

    statistic, p_value = mannwhitneyu(
        group_0,
        group_1,
        alternative="two-sided",
    )

    # Rank-biserial correlation: positive values indicate larger observations
    # when the characteristic is present.
    rank_biserial = (
        1 - (2 * statistic) / (len(group_1) * len(group_0))
    )

    mann_whitney_results.append({
        "Variable": variable,
        "N (0)": len(group_0),
        "Median (0)": group_0.median(),
        "N (1)": len(group_1),
        "Median (1)": group_1.median(),
        "U Statistic": statistic,
        "P-Value": p_value,
        "Rank-Biserial Correlation": rank_biserial,
    })

mann_whitney_table = (
    pd.DataFrame(mann_whitney_results)
    .sort_values("P-Value")
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

mann_whitney_table["FDR-Adjusted P-Value"] = multipletests(
    mann_whitney_table["P-Value"],
    method="fdr_bh",
)[1]

mann_whitney_table["Significant after FDR Adjustment"] = (
    mann_whitney_table["FDR-Adjusted P-Value"] < 0.05
)

display(
    mann_whitney_table.style
    .format({
        "Median (0)": "{:,.0f}",
        "Median (1)": "{:,.0f}",
        "U Statistic": "{:,.0f}",
        "P-Value": format_p_value,
        "FDR-Adjusted P-Value": "{:.4f}",
        "Rank-Biserial Correlation": "{:.3f}",
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

## Nonparametric Summary

The statistically significant Mann–Whitney comparisons are summarized below to
show which binary characteristics are associated with differences in reported
breach size.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-nonparametric-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of statistically significant breach-size comparisons"
#| echo: false

nonparametric_summary = (
    mann_whitney_table
    .loc[
        mann_whitney_table["P-Value"] < 0.05,
        ["Variable", "Median (0)", "Median (1)", "P-Value"],
    ]
    .copy()
)

nonparametric_summary["Higher Median Group"] = np.where(
    nonparametric_summary["Median (1)"] >
    nonparametric_summary["Median (0)"],
    "Present (1)",
    "Absent (0)",
)

display(
    nonparametric_summary.style
    .format({
        "Median (0)": "{:,.0f}",
        "Median (1)": "{:,.0f}",
        "P-Value": "{:.4f}",
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

The summary identifies characteristics associated with differences in breach
size at the bivariate level. These comparisons are descriptive associations
and do not account for other breach characteristics simultaneously.

## Covered Entity Type Comparison

Breach-size distributions are compared across covered entity types using the
Kruskal–Wallis test. Group-level summaries provide context for differences in
breach frequency, median breach size, and severe-breach prevalence.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-entity-type-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Breach characteristics by covered entity type"
#| echo: false

entity_summary = (
    analysis_data
    .dropna(subset=["Covered_Entity_Type"])
    .groupby("Covered_Entity_Type")
    .agg(
        Breaches=("Record_ID", "count"),
        Median_Affected=("Individuals_Affected", "median"),
        Severe_Breaches=("Large_Breach_100K", "sum"),
        Known_Outcomes=("Large_Breach_100K", "count"),
    )
    .reset_index()
)

entity_summary["Severe_Rate"] = (
    entity_summary["Severe_Breaches"]
    / entity_summary["Known_Outcomes"]
    * 100
)

display(
    entity_summary.style
    .format({
        "Median_Affected": "{:,.0f}",
        "Severe_Breaches": "{:,.0f}",
        "Severe_Rate": "{:.2f}%",
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-kruskal-entity-type
#| output: false
#| tbl-cap: "Kruskal–Wallis comparison of breach size across covered entity types"
#| echo: false

entity_groups = [
    group["Individuals_Affected"].dropna()
    for _, group in analysis_data.groupby("Covered_Entity_Type")
    if group["Individuals_Affected"].notna().any()
]

kruskal_statistic, kruskal_p_value = kruskal(
    *entity_groups,
    nan_policy="omit",
)

kruskal_result = pd.DataFrame({
    "Statistic": [
        "Kruskal–Wallis H",
        "Degrees of Freedom",
        "P-Value",
    ],
    "Value": [
        kruskal_statistic,
        len(entity_groups) - 1,
        kruskal_p_value,
    ],
})

display(kruskal_result.round(4))
```

The Kruskal–Wallis test evaluates whether breach-size distributions differ
across covered entity types. A statistically significant result indicates that
at least one entity-type distribution differs from the others but does not, by
itself, identify which specific groups differ.

# Exploratory Breach-Profile Clustering

## Purpose and Feature Selection

An exploratory cluster analysis is used to identify recurring combinations of
reported breach characteristics. Unlike logistic regression, clustering does
not estimate the probability of a severe breach or test a causal relationship.
Its purpose is to organize similar breach records into descriptive profiles.

The clustering features include breach-type indicators, information-location
indicators, business-associate involvement, covered entity type, and submission
year. Breach size and severe-breach status are excluded from cluster formation.
This separation allows the resulting clusters to be compared on breach severity
afterward without using the outcome to construct the groups.

## Clustering Dataset

```{python}
#| label: prepare-clustering-data
#| echo: true

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler

cluster_binary_features = binary_predictors.copy()

cluster_source = analysis_data[
    [
        "Record_ID",
        "Submission_Year",
        "Covered_Entity_Type",
        *cluster_binary_features,
    ]
].copy()

cluster_source["Covered_Entity_Type"] = (
    cluster_source["Covered_Entity_Type"]
    .fillna("Unknown")
    .astype(str)
    .str.strip()
    .replace("", "Unknown")
)

cluster_source["Submission_Year"] = (
    pd.to_numeric(
        cluster_source["Submission_Year"],
        errors="coerce",
    )
    .fillna(
        cluster_source["Submission_Year"].median()
    )
)

entity_dummies = pd.get_dummies(
    cluster_source["Covered_Entity_Type"],
    prefix="Entity",
    dtype=float,
)

year_scaler = MinMaxScaler()

scaled_year = year_scaler.fit_transform(
    cluster_source[["Submission_Year"]]
)

cluster_features = pd.concat(
    [
        pd.DataFrame(
            scaled_year,
            columns=["Submission_Year_Scaled"],
            index=cluster_source.index,
        ),
        cluster_source[
            cluster_binary_features
        ].astype(float),
        entity_dummies,
    ],
    axis=1,
)

print(f"Clustering observations: {len(cluster_features):,}")
print(f"Clustering features: {cluster_features.shape[1]:,}")
print(
    "Missing clustering values:",
    int(cluster_features.isna().sum().sum()),
)
```

## Number of Clusters

Candidate solutions containing two through six clusters are evaluated using
inertia and the silhouette coefficient. Inertia measures within-cluster
dispersion, while the silhouette coefficient describes how closely each record
matches its assigned cluster relative to neighboring clusters.

The silhouette coefficient ranges from \(-1\) to \(1\), with larger values
indicating clearer separation. Because this is an exploratory analysis, the
selected solution should balance quantitative separation with substantive
interpretability.

```{python}
#| label: evaluate-cluster-solutions
#| output: false
#| echo: false

cluster_evaluation = []

candidate_clusters = range(2, 7)

for number_of_clusters in candidate_clusters:
    candidate_model = KMeans(
        n_clusters=number_of_clusters,
        random_state=42,
        n_init=20,
    )

    candidate_labels = candidate_model.fit_predict(
        cluster_features
    )

    silhouette = silhouette_score(
        cluster_features,
        candidate_labels,
        sample_size=min(
            2_000,
            len(cluster_features),
        ),
        random_state=42,
    )

    cluster_evaluation.append({
        "Clusters": number_of_clusters,
        "Inertia": candidate_model.inertia_,
        "Silhouette Score": silhouette,
    })

cluster_evaluation = pd.DataFrame(
    cluster_evaluation
)

display(
    cluster_evaluation.style
    .format({
        "Inertia": "{:,.2f}",
        "Silhouette Score": "{:.3f}",
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-cluster-selection
#| fig-cap: "Evaluation of candidate breach-profile cluster solutions"
#| fig-alt: "Two-panel cluster evaluation showing declining within-cluster inertia and the highest silhouette coefficient at five clusters."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| echo: false

fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    1,
    2,
    figsize=(11, 4.5),
)

sns.lineplot(
    data=cluster_evaluation,
    x="Clusters",
    y="Inertia",
    marker="o",
    linewidth=2,
    color=REPORT_COLORS["blue"],
    ax=axes[0],
)
axes[0].set_title("Within-Cluster Inertia")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Number of Clusters")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Inertia")

sns.lineplot(
    data=cluster_evaluation,
    x="Clusters",
    y="Silhouette Score",
    marker="o",
    linewidth=2,
    color=REPORT_COLORS["teal"],
    ax=axes[1],
)
axes[1].set_title("Silhouette Coefficient")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Number of Clusters")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Silhouette Score")

for axis in axes:
    axis.set_xticks(
        list(candidate_clusters)
    )
    axis.spines["top"].set_visible(False)
    axis.spines["right"].set_visible(False)
    axis.grid(
        alpha=0.20,
    )

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Selected Cluster Solution

The solution with the highest silhouette coefficient is selected
programmatically. A fixed random seed and multiple initializations are used to
improve reproducibility.

```{python}
#| label: fit-selected-clusters
#| echo: true

selected_k = int(
    cluster_evaluation.loc[
        cluster_evaluation["Silhouette Score"].idxmax(),
        "Clusters",
    ]
)

cluster_model = KMeans(
    n_clusters=selected_k,
    random_state=42,
    n_init=50,
)

analysis_data["Cluster"] = (
    cluster_model.fit_predict(
        cluster_features
    )
    + 1
)

analysis_data["Cluster"] = (
    "Cluster "
    + analysis_data["Cluster"].astype(str)
)

print(f"Selected number of clusters: {selected_k}")
print(
    "Selected silhouette score:",
    f"{cluster_evaluation.loc[cluster_evaluation['Clusters'].eq(selected_k), 'Silhouette Score'].iloc[0]:.3f}",
)
```

## Cluster Sizes and Outcomes

Cluster membership is summarized before examining each profile's defining
features. Severe-breach prevalence and breach size are calculated after cluster
formation and were not inputs to the clustering algorithm.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cluster-outcomes
#| tbl-cap: "Size and breach outcomes of the exploratory clusters"
#| echo: false

cluster_outcomes = (
    analysis_data
    .groupby(
        "Cluster",
        as_index=False,
    )
    .agg(
        Breaches=("Record_ID", "count"),
        Median_Affected=("Individuals_Affected", "median"),
        Severe_Breaches=("Large_Breach_100K", "sum"),
        Known_Outcomes=("Large_Breach_100K", "count"),
    )
)

cluster_outcomes["Percent of Sample"] = (
    cluster_outcomes["Breaches"]
    / len(analysis_data)
    * 100
)

cluster_outcomes["Severe Rate"] = np.where(
    cluster_outcomes["Known_Outcomes"] > 0,
    cluster_outcomes["Severe_Breaches"]
    / cluster_outcomes["Known_Outcomes"]
    * 100,
    np.nan,
)

cluster_outcomes = (
    cluster_outcomes
    .sort_values("Cluster")
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

display(
    cluster_outcomes[
        [
            "Cluster",
            "Breaches",
            "Percent of Sample",
            "Median_Affected",
            "Severe_Breaches",
            "Severe Rate",
        ]
    ]
    .style
    .format({
        "Breaches": "{:,.0f}",
        "Percent of Sample": "{:.2f}%",
        "Median_Affected": "{:,.0f}",
        "Severe_Breaches": "{:,.0f}",
        "Severe Rate": "{:.2f}%",
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

## Cluster Characteristic Profiles

The following table reports the percentage of breaches within each cluster that
contain each binary characteristic. Larger percentages identify the
characteristics that are most prominent within a cluster.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cluster-binary-profile
#| output: false
#| tbl-cap: "Prevalence of binary breach characteristics within each cluster"
#| echo: false

cluster_binary_profile = (
    analysis_data
    .groupby("Cluster")[
        cluster_binary_features
    ]
    .mean()
    .mul(100)
    .round(2)
    .reset_index()
)

display(
    cluster_binary_profile.style
    .format({
        variable: "{:.2f}%"
        for variable in cluster_binary_features
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

## Covered Entity Composition by Cluster

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cluster-entity-profile
#| output: false
#| tbl-cap: "Covered entity composition within each cluster"
#| echo: false

cluster_entity_profile = (
    analysis_data
    .assign(
        Covered_Entity_Type=(
            analysis_data["Covered_Entity_Type"]
            .fillna("Unknown")
            .astype(str)
            .str.strip()
            .replace("", "Unknown")
        )
    )
    .groupby(
        ["Cluster", "Covered_Entity_Type"]
    )
    .size()
    .rename("Breaches")
    .reset_index()
)

cluster_entity_profile["Cluster Total"] = (
    cluster_entity_profile
    .groupby("Cluster")["Breaches"]
    .transform("sum")
)

cluster_entity_profile["Within-Cluster Percent"] = (
    cluster_entity_profile["Breaches"]
    / cluster_entity_profile["Cluster Total"]
    * 100
)

display(
    cluster_entity_profile[
        [
            "Cluster",
            "Covered_Entity_Type",
            "Breaches",
            "Within-Cluster Percent",
        ]
    ]
    .sort_values(
        ["Cluster", "Within-Cluster Percent"],
        ascending=[True, False],
    )
    .style
    .format({
        "Breaches": "{:,.0f}",
        "Within-Cluster Percent": "{:.2f}%",
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

## Dominant Characteristics

To support interpretation, each cluster is summarized using its three most
prevalent binary characteristics. These descriptions are data-derived profile
labels rather than predefined breach categories.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cluster-dominant-features
#| output: false
#| tbl-cap: "Dominant binary characteristics of each exploratory cluster"
#| echo: false

dominant_feature_results = []

cluster_means = (
    analysis_data
    .groupby("Cluster")[
        cluster_binary_features
    ]
    .mean()
)

for cluster_name, row in cluster_means.iterrows():
    top_features = (
        row
        .sort_values(ascending=False)
        .head(3)
    )

    dominant_feature_results.append({
        "Cluster": cluster_name,
        "Most Prevalent Characteristic": (
            top_features.index[0]
        ),
        "Prevalence 1": (
            top_features.iloc[0] * 100
        ),
        "Second Characteristic": (
            top_features.index[1]
        ),
        "Prevalence 2": (
            top_features.iloc[1] * 100
        ),
        "Third Characteristic": (
            top_features.index[2]
        ),
        "Prevalence 3": (
            top_features.iloc[2] * 100
        ),
    })

dominant_features = pd.DataFrame(
    dominant_feature_results
)

display(
    dominant_features.style
    .format({
        "Prevalence 1": "{:.2f}%",
        "Prevalence 2": "{:.2f}%",
        "Prevalence 3": "{:.2f}%",
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

The clusters describe recurring combinations of breach characteristics rather
than natural or definitive classes. Differences in severe-breach prevalence
across clusters are descriptive and should be interpreted alongside the
individual predictors evaluated in the logistic-regression model.

Because K-means relies on Euclidean distance, the analysis should be treated as an interpretable exploratory segmentation of the encoded breach
characteristics—not as evidence that the records possess a single objectively correct cluster structure.

## Interpreted Breach Profiles

Based on the prevalence of breach characteristics and covered entity types,
descriptive names are assigned to the five clusters. These labels summarize the
dominant characteristics and do not represent official HHS breach categories.

```{python}
#| label: assign-cluster-profile-labels
#| echo: true

cluster_profile_labels = {
    "Cluster 1": (
        "Provider Hacking and Network-Server Breaches"
    ),
    "Cluster 2": (
        "Business-Associate Hacking and Network-Server Breaches"
    ),
    "Cluster 3": (
        "Provider Unauthorized-Access Breaches"
    ),
    "Cluster 4": (
        "Health-Plan Mixed Digital Breaches"
    ),
    "Cluster 5": (
        "Provider Theft and Physical-Record Breaches"
    ),
}

analysis_data["Cluster_Profile"] = (
    analysis_data["Cluster"]
    .map(cluster_profile_labels)
)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-interpreted-cluster-profiles
#| tbl-cap: "Interpreted breach profiles and observed severity outcomes"
#| echo: false

interpreted_cluster_summary = (
    cluster_outcomes
    .assign(
        Profile=cluster_outcomes["Cluster"]
        .map(cluster_profile_labels)
    )
    [
        [
            "Cluster",
            "Profile",
            "Breaches",
            "Percent of Sample",
            "Median_Affected",
            "Severe_Breaches",
            "Severe Rate",
        ]
    ]
)

display(
    interpreted_cluster_summary.style
    .format({
        "Breaches": "{:,.0f}",
        "Percent of Sample": "{:.2f}%",
        "Median_Affected": "{:,.0f}",
        "Severe_Breaches": "{:,.0f}",
        "Severe Rate": "{:.2f}%",
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

The five-cluster solution produced a silhouette coefficient of \(0.390\),
indicating moderate separation among the exploratory breach profiles. The
clusters primarily distinguish covered entity type, breach mechanism,
information location, and business-associate involvement.

The Business-Associate Hacking and Network-Server profile had the highest
observed severe-breach rate at 17.77%, followed by the Provider Hacking and
Network-Server profile at 13.43%. Together, these findings reinforce the
importance of network-facing infrastructure and third-party security
relationships when prioritizing security capabilities.

The Provider Unauthorized-Access profile and Provider Theft and
Physical-Record profile had substantially lower severe-breach rates of 1.85%
and 1.99%, respectively. These clusters remain operationally important, but
their reported incidents were less likely to cross the study's
100,000-person severity threshold.

The clustering results complement—but do not replace—the inferential analysis.
Cluster membership is not included as a logistic-regression predictor because
the clusters were derived from the same breach characteristics already entered
into the model. Including both would introduce redundancy and complicate
coefficient interpretation.


# Logistic Regression

## Predictor Review

Before fitting the multivariable logistic regression, candidate predictors are
reviewed for overlap and redundancy. Breach-type indicators may overlap because
a single record can contain more than one breach classification, while the final
regression model requires a clearer and more interpretable reference structure.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-predictor-review
#| output: false
#| tbl-cap: "Frequency and overlap review for candidate logistic-regression predictors"
#| echo: false

predictor_review = pd.DataFrame({
    "Predictor": binary_predictors,
    "Present": [
        analysis_data[variable].eq(1).sum()
        for variable in binary_predictors
    ],
})

predictor_review["Percent Present"] = (
    predictor_review["Present"] / len(analysis_data) * 100
).round(2)

display(predictor_review)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-breach-type-overlap
#| output: false
#| tbl-cap: "Overlap among breach-type indicators"
#| echo: false

breach_type_indicators = [
    "Breach_Hacking_IT",
    "Breach_Unauthorized_Access",
    "Breach_Theft",
    "Breach_Loss",
    "Breach_Improper_Disposal",
]

breach_type_overlap = (
    analysis_data[breach_type_indicators]
    .sum(axis=1)
    .value_counts()
    .sort_index()
    .rename_axis("Number of Breach-Type Indicators")
    .reset_index(name="Records")
)

breach_type_overlap["Percent"] = (
    breach_type_overlap["Records"] / len(analysis_data) * 100
).round(2)

display(breach_type_overlap)
```

The overlap review confirms that the breach-type indicators are not mutually
exclusive. For the final logistic regression, breach type is therefore recoded
into a single mutually exclusive categorical variable so that each record
belongs to one breach-type category.

## Mutually Exclusive Breach-Type Coding

Because the original breach-type field may contain multiple classifications,
a mutually exclusive breach-type variable is created for logistic regression.
Hacking/IT Incident serves as the reference category because it is the most
frequent breach type and provides a meaningful comparison for the remaining
categories.

```{python}
#| label: create-breach-type-model
#| echo: true

breach_type_text = (
    analysis_data["Breach_Type"]
    .fillna("")
    .astype(str)
)

conditions = [
    breach_type_text.str.contains(
        "Hacking/IT Incident",
        case=False,
        regex=False,
    ),
    breach_type_text.str.contains(
        "Unauthorized Access/Disclosure",
        case=False,
        regex=False,
    ),
    breach_type_text.str.contains("Theft", case=False, regex=False),
    breach_type_text.str.contains("Loss", case=False, regex=False),
    breach_type_text.str.contains(
        "Improper Disposal",
        case=False,
        regex=False,
    ),
]

categories = [
    "Hacking/IT",
    "Unauthorized",
    "Theft",
    "Loss",
    "Improper Disposal",
]

analysis_data["Breach_Type_Model"] = np.select(
    conditions,
    categories,
    default="Other / Multiple",
)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-breach-type-model
#| output: false
#| tbl-cap: "Mutually exclusive breach-type categories used in logistic regression"
#| echo: false

breach_type_model_summary = (
    analysis_data["Breach_Type_Model"]
    .value_counts()
    .reindex([
        "Hacking/IT",
        "Unauthorized",
        "Theft",
        "Loss",
        "Improper Disposal",
        "Other / Multiple",
    ], fill_value=0)
    .rename_axis("Breach Type")
    .reset_index(name="Records")
)

breach_type_model_summary["Percent"] = (
    breach_type_model_summary["Records"]
    / len(analysis_data)
    * 100
).round(2)

display(breach_type_model_summary)
```

Each record is assigned to one category. Records containing Hacking/IT Incident
are classified as Hacking/IT first; the remaining categories are assigned in
the order shown above. Records not captured by these categories, including
remaining multiple-type combinations, are grouped as Other / Multiple.

## Model Specification

A multivariable logistic regression estimates the adjusted association between
observable breach characteristics and the probability that a reported breach
is severe. The outcome equals 1 when at least 100,000 individuals are affected
and 0 otherwise.

The model includes mutually exclusive breach type, covered entity type,
information-location indicators, and business-associate involvement.

$$
\operatorname{logit}\left[P(Y_i=1)\right]
=
\beta_0
+
\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j X_{ij}
$$

where \(Y_i\) indicates severe-breach status and \(X_{ij}\) represents the
included breach characteristics.

```{python}
#| label: fit-logistic-model
#| echo: true

import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

model_columns = [
    "Large_Breach_100K",
    "Breach_Type_Model",
    "Covered_Entity_Type",
    "Location_Desktop",
    "Location_EMR",
    "Location_Laptop",
    "Location_Network_Server",
    "Location_Paper",
    "Location_Portable_Device",
    "Business_Associate_Yes",
]

logit_data = analysis_data[model_columns].dropna().copy()

logit_formula = """
Large_Breach_100K ~
C(Breach_Type_Model, Treatment(reference='Hacking/IT')) +
C(Covered_Entity_Type, Treatment(reference='Healthcare Provider')) +
Location_Desktop +
Location_EMR +
Location_Laptop +
Location_Network_Server +
Location_Paper +
Location_Portable_Device +
Business_Associate_Yes
"""

logit_model = smf.logit(
    formula=logit_formula,
    data=logit_data,
).fit(disp=False)

print(f"Model observations: {int(logit_model.nobs):,}")
print(f"Converged: {logit_model.mle_retvals['converged']}")
print(f"McFadden pseudo-R²: {logit_model.prsquared:.4f}")
print(f"Log-likelihood: {logit_model.llf:.3f}")
print(f"Null log-likelihood: {logit_model.llnull:.3f}")
print(f"Likelihood-ratio p-value: {logit_model.llr_pvalue:.4g}")
```

## Variance Inflation Factor

Variance inflation factors are calculated for the final predictor set to assess
whether multicollinearity is likely to affect coefficient stability.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-vif
#| output: false
#| tbl-cap: "Variance inflation factors for logistic-regression predictors"
#| echo: false

from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor

design_matrix = pd.get_dummies(
    logit_data.drop(columns=["Large_Breach_100K"]),
    columns=[
        "Breach_Type_Model",
        "Covered_Entity_Type",
    ],
    drop_first=True,
    dtype=float,
)

vif_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Predictor": design_matrix.columns,
    "VIF": [
        variance_inflation_factor(design_matrix.values, i)
        for i in range(design_matrix.shape[1])
    ],
})

vif_table = (
    vif_results
    .sort_values("VIF", ascending=False)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

display(vif_table.round({"VIF": 3}))
```

The VIF values are low across the final predictor set, indicating that
multicollinearity is not a material concern for interpretation of the fitted
model.

## Adjusted Odds Ratios

Logistic-regression coefficients are exponentiated to obtain adjusted odds
ratios. An odds ratio above 1 indicates higher adjusted odds of a severe breach,
while an odds ratio below 1 indicates lower adjusted odds relative to the
applicable reference category or indicator-absent group.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-adjusted-odds-ratios
#| tbl-cap: "Adjusted odds ratios for severe-breach status"
#| echo: false

confidence_intervals = logit_model.conf_int()

odds_ratio_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Predictor": logit_model.params.index,
    "Adjusted Odds Ratio": np.exp(logit_model.params),
    "95% CI Lower": np.exp(confidence_intervals[0]),
    "95% CI Upper": np.exp(confidence_intervals[1]),
    "P-Value": logit_model.pvalues,
}).reset_index(drop=True)

odds_ratio_table = (
    odds_ratio_table
    .loc[odds_ratio_table["Predictor"] != "Intercept"]
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

predictor_labels = {
    "C(Breach_Type_Model, Treatment(reference='Hacking/IT'))[T.Improper Disposal]":
        "Improper disposal vs Hacking/IT",
    "C(Breach_Type_Model, Treatment(reference='Hacking/IT'))[T.Loss]":
        "Loss vs Hacking/IT",
    "C(Breach_Type_Model, Treatment(reference='Hacking/IT'))[T.Other / Multiple]":
        "Other or multiple types vs Hacking/IT",
    "C(Breach_Type_Model, Treatment(reference='Hacking/IT'))[T.Theft]":
        "Theft vs Hacking/IT",
    "C(Breach_Type_Model, Treatment(reference='Hacking/IT'))[T.Unauthorized]":
        "Unauthorized access/disclosure vs Hacking/IT",
    "C(Covered_Entity_Type, Treatment(reference='Healthcare Provider'))[T.Business Associate]":
        "Business associate vs Healthcare provider",
    "C(Covered_Entity_Type, Treatment(reference='Healthcare Provider'))[T.Health Plan]":
        "Health plan vs Healthcare provider",
    "C(Covered_Entity_Type, Treatment(reference='Healthcare Provider'))[T.Healthcare Clearing House]":
        "Healthcare clearinghouse vs Healthcare provider",
    "Location_Desktop": "Desktop involved: Yes vs No",
    "Location_EMR": "Electronic medical record involved: Yes vs No",
    "Location_Laptop": "Laptop involved: Yes vs No",
    "Location_Network_Server": "Network server involved: Yes vs No",
    "Location_Paper": "Paper records involved: Yes vs No",
    "Location_Portable_Device": "Portable device involved: Yes vs No",
    "Business_Associate_Yes": "Business associate involved: Yes vs No",
}

odds_ratio_table["Predictor"] = (
    odds_ratio_table["Predictor"]
    .replace(predictor_labels)
)

odds_ratio_table["Significant at 0.05"] = (
    odds_ratio_table["P-Value"] < 0.05
).map({True: "Yes", False: "No"})

display(
    odds_ratio_table.style
    .format({
        "Adjusted Odds Ratio": "{:.3f}",
        "95% CI Lower": "{:.3f}",
        "95% CI Upper": "{:.3f}",
        "P-Value": format_p_value,
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

Several adjusted associations are especially relevant to the architecture
analysis. Network-server involvement is associated with substantially higher
odds of a severe breach, while paper records are associated with lower odds.
Covered entities classified as business associates also show higher adjusted
odds relative to healthcare providers. These estimates represent associations
within the reported breach data and should not be interpreted as causal effects.

## Model Fit and Statistical Significance

Model fit is summarized using the log-likelihood, McFadden pseudo-\(R^2\), and
likelihood-ratio test.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-model-fit
#| tbl-cap: "Logistic-regression model fit"
#| echo: false

model_fit = pd.DataFrame({
    "Measure": [
        "Observations",
        "Log-Likelihood",
        "Null Log-Likelihood",
        "McFadden Pseudo-R²",
        "Likelihood-Ratio Chi-Square",
        "Likelihood-Ratio P-Value",
        "Converged",
    ],
    "Value": [
        f"{int(logit_model.nobs):,}",
        f"{logit_model.llf:.3f}",
        f"{logit_model.llnull:.3f}",
        f"{logit_model.prsquared:.4f}",
        f"{logit_model.llr:.3f}",
        format_p_value(logit_model.llr_pvalue),
        "Yes" if logit_model.mle_retvals["converged"] else "No",
    ],
})

display(model_fit.style.hide(axis="index"))
```

The likelihood-ratio test evaluates improvement over the intercept-only model.
McFadden pseudo-\(R^2\) is not interpreted as variance explained.

## In-Sample Classification Diagnostics

In-sample metrics describe the fitted model but are not treated as estimates of
out-of-sample performance.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-in-sample-performance
#| output: false
#| tbl-cap: "In-sample logistic-regression classification performance"
#| echo: false

from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score,
    confusion_matrix,
    f1_score,
    precision_score,
    recall_score,
    roc_auc_score,
)

in_sample_probability = logit_model.predict(logit_data)
in_sample_prediction = (in_sample_probability >= 0.50).astype(int)

y_observed = logit_data["Large_Breach_100K"].astype(int)

tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(
    y_observed,
    in_sample_prediction,
).ravel()

in_sample_metrics = pd.DataFrame({
    "Metric": [
        "ROC-AUC",
        "Accuracy",
        "Sensitivity",
        "Specificity",
        "Precision",
        "F1 Score",
        "True Negatives",
        "False Positives",
        "False Negatives",
        "True Positives",
    ],
    "Value": [
        roc_auc_score(y_observed, in_sample_probability),
        accuracy_score(y_observed, in_sample_prediction),
        recall_score(y_observed, in_sample_prediction),
        tn / (tn + fp),
        precision_score(y_observed, in_sample_prediction, zero_division=0),
        f1_score(y_observed, in_sample_prediction, zero_division=0),
        tn,
        fp,
        fn,
        tp,
    ],
})

display(
    in_sample_metrics.style
    .format({"Value": "{:.4f}"})
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

The 0.50 classification threshold provides a conventional initial diagnostic,
but it is not assumed to be the most appropriate operating threshold for the
imbalanced severe-breach outcome. Threshold selection is evaluated separately
below.

## Threshold Analysis

Because the severe-breach outcome is imbalanced, the conventional 0.50 cutoff
is compared with a threshold selected using Youden's \(J\) statistic.

$$
J = \text{Sensitivity} + \text{Specificity} - 1
$$

```{python}
#| label: cell-threshold-analysis
#| output: false
#| echo: false

from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve

false_positive_rate, true_positive_rate, thresholds = roc_curve(
    y_observed,
    in_sample_probability,
)

youden_j = true_positive_rate - false_positive_rate
best_index = np.argmax(youden_j)
in_sample_threshold = thresholds[best_index]

threshold_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Measure": [
        "Selected Threshold",
        "Sensitivity",
        "Specificity",
        "Youden's J",
    ],
    "Value": [
        in_sample_threshold,
        true_positive_rate[best_index],
        1 - false_positive_rate[best_index],
        youden_j[best_index],
    ],
})

display(
    threshold_summary.style
    .format({"Value": "{:.4f}"})
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-threshold-performance
#| output: false
#| tbl-cap: "In-sample classification performance at the Youden-selected threshold"
#| echo: false

threshold_prediction = (
    in_sample_probability >= in_sample_threshold
).astype(int)

tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(
    y_observed,
    threshold_prediction,
).ravel()

threshold_performance = pd.DataFrame({
    "Metric": [
        "Sensitivity",
        "Specificity",
        "Precision",
        "F1 Score",
        "True Negatives",
        "False Positives",
        "False Negatives",
        "True Positives",
    ],
    "Value": [
        recall_score(y_observed, threshold_prediction),
        tn / (tn + fp),
        precision_score(
            y_observed,
            threshold_prediction,
            zero_division=0,
        ),
        f1_score(
            y_observed,
            threshold_prediction,
            zero_division=0,
        ),
        tn,
        fp,
        fn,
        tp,
    ],
})

display(
    threshold_performance.style
    .format({"Value": "{:.4f}"})
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-threshold-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of conventional and Youden-selected thresholds"
#| echo: false

conventional_tn, conventional_fp, _, _ = confusion_matrix(
    y_observed,
    in_sample_prediction,
).ravel()

selected_tn, selected_fp, _, _ = confusion_matrix(
    y_observed,
    threshold_prediction,
).ravel()

threshold_comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "Threshold": ["Conventional 0.50", "Youden-Selected"],
    "Cutoff": [0.50, in_sample_threshold],
    "Sensitivity": [
        recall_score(y_observed, in_sample_prediction),
        recall_score(y_observed, threshold_prediction),
    ],
    "Specificity": [
        conventional_tn / (conventional_tn + conventional_fp),
        selected_tn / (selected_tn + selected_fp),
    ],
    "Precision": [
        precision_score(y_observed, in_sample_prediction, zero_division=0),
        precision_score(y_observed, threshold_prediction, zero_division=0),
    ],
})

display(
    threshold_comparison.style
    .format({
        "Cutoff": "{:.4f}",
        "Sensitivity": "{:.4f}",
        "Specificity": "{:.4f}",
        "Precision": "{:.4f}",
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

The lower threshold increases sensitivity to severe breaches at the cost of
specificity and precision.

# Holdout Validation

Out-of-sample performance is evaluated on observations not used for model
fitting or threshold selection.

## Stratified Train-Test Split

A stratified 80/20 train-test split preserves severe-breach prevalence across
samples. Random seed 42 is used for reproducibility.

```{python}
#| label: holdout-split
#| output: false
#| echo: true

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

train_data, test_data = train_test_split(
    logit_data,
    test_size=0.20,
    stratify=logit_data["Large_Breach_100K"],
    random_state=42,
)

split_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Sample": ["Training", "Test"],
    "N": [len(train_data), len(test_data)],
    "Severe Breaches": [
        train_data["Large_Breach_100K"].sum(),
        test_data["Large_Breach_100K"].sum(),
    ],
})

split_summary["Severe Rate (%)"] = (
    split_summary["Severe Breaches"]
    / split_summary["N"]
    * 100
)

display(
    split_summary.style
    .format({
        "Severe Breaches": "{:,.0f}",
        "Severe Rate (%)": "{:.2f}%",
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

## Training Model and Threshold Selection

The logistic-regression specification is refitted using only the training
sample. Youden's \(J\) statistic is then calculated from training predictions
to select the classification threshold without using test outcomes.

```{python}
#| label: training-model-threshold
#| output: false
#| echo: false

training_model = smf.logit(
    formula=logit_formula,
    data=train_data,
).fit(disp=False)

y_train = train_data["Large_Breach_100K"].astype(int)
train_probability = training_model.predict(train_data)

train_fpr, train_tpr, train_thresholds = roc_curve(
    y_train,
    train_probability,
)

train_youden_j = train_tpr - train_fpr
train_best_index = np.argmax(train_youden_j)
selected_threshold = train_thresholds[train_best_index]

training_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Measure": [
        "Training Observations",
        "Training Severe Rate",
        "Training ROC-AUC",
        "Selected Threshold",
        "Sensitivity at Threshold",
        "Specificity at Threshold",
        "Youden's J",
    ],
    "Value": [
        len(train_data),
        y_train.mean(),
        roc_auc_score(y_train, train_probability),
        selected_threshold,
        train_tpr[train_best_index],
        1 - train_fpr[train_best_index],
        train_youden_j[train_best_index],
    ],
})

display(
    training_summary.style
    .format({"Value": "{:.4f}"})
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

## Five-Fold Cross-Validation

Five-fold stratified cross-validation is applied to the training sample to
assess the stability of ROC-AUC across resampled validation folds. The held-out
test sample remains untouched.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cross-validation-auc
#| tbl-cap: "Five-fold stratified cross-validation ROC-AUC on the training sample"
#| echo: false

from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold

cv = StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=42,
)

cv_results = []

for fold, (fit_index, validation_index) in enumerate(
    cv.split(
        train_data,
        train_data["Large_Breach_100K"],
    ),
    start=1,
):
    fold_train = train_data.iloc[fit_index].copy()
    fold_validation = train_data.iloc[validation_index].copy()

    fold_model = smf.logit(
        formula=logit_formula,
        data=fold_train,
    ).fit(
        method="lbfgs",
        maxiter=1000,
        disp=False,
    )

    fold_probability = fold_model.predict(
        fold_validation
    )

    fold_auc = roc_auc_score(
        fold_validation["Large_Breach_100K"],
        fold_probability,
    )

    cv_results.append({
        "Fold": fold,
        "ROC-AUC": fold_auc,
        "Converged": fold_model.mle_retvals["converged"],
        "Iterations": fold_model.mle_retvals.get("iterations", np.nan),
    })

cv_results = pd.DataFrame(cv_results)

cv_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Measure": [
        "Mean ROC-AUC",
        "Standard Deviation",
        "Minimum ROC-AUC",
        "Maximum ROC-AUC",
        "Converged Folds",
    ],
    "Value": [
        cv_results["ROC-AUC"].mean(),
        cv_results["ROC-AUC"].std(ddof=1),
        cv_results["ROC-AUC"].min(),
        cv_results["ROC-AUC"].max(),
        int(cv_results["Converged"].sum()),
    ],
})

display(
    cv_summary.style
    .format({
        "Value": lambda value: (
            f"{int(value)}"
            if float(value).is_integer() and value > 1
            else f"{value:.4f}"
        )
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

The cross-validation results provide a resampling-based check of discrimination
stability within the training sample. Convergence status is reported for each
fold so that ROC-AUC results are interpreted only from successfully fitted
models.

## Training vs Test Discrimination

ROC-AUC is compared between the training and held-out test samples.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-training-test-discrimination
#| tbl-cap: "Training and held-out discrimination"
#| echo: false

y_test = test_data["Large_Breach_100K"].astype(int)
test_probability = training_model.predict(test_data)

discrimination_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Sample": ["Training", "Held-Out Test"],
    "ROC-AUC": [
        roc_auc_score(y_train, train_probability),
        roc_auc_score(y_test, test_probability),
    ],
})

display(
    discrimination_summary.style
    .format({"ROC-AUC": "{:.4f}"})
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

Similar training and test ROC-AUC values indicate that discrimination is
stable across the holdout split.

## Held-Out Classification Performance

The training-derived threshold is applied unchanged to the held-out test sample.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-holdout-threshold-performance
#| tbl-cap: "Held-out classification performance at the training-derived threshold"
#| echo: false

test_prediction = (
    test_probability >= selected_threshold
).astype(int)

tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(
    y_test,
    test_prediction,

test_sensitivity = recall_score(
    y_test,

)

test_specificity = tn / (tn + fp)

    y_test,
    test_prediction,
    zero_division=0,
)

test_f1 = f1_score(
    y_test,
    test_prediction,
    zero_division=0,
)

holdout_performance = pd.DataFrame({
    "Metric": [
        "Selected Threshold",
        "Sensitivity",
        "Specificity",
        "Precision",
        "F1 Score",
        "True Negatives",
        "False Positives",
        "False Negatives",
        "True Positives",
    ],
    "Value": [
        selected_threshold,
        test_sensitivity,
        test_specificity,
        test_precision,
        test_f1,
        tn,
        fp,
        fn,
        tp,
    ],
})

display(
    holdout_performance.style
    .format({
        "Value": lambda value: (
            f"{value:.4f}"
            if isinstance(value, (float, np.floating))
            else f"{value:,}"
        )
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

The training-derived threshold favors sensitivity to severe breaches, with
lower precision under the imbalanced outcome.

```{python}
#| label: fig-calibration
```

# NIST-Aligned Architecture Assessment

Observed risk signals are mapped to NIST-aligned security capabilities and
evaluated using eight decision criteria.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-architecture-criteria
#| tbl-cap: "Criteria used to evaluate candidate security-architecture capabilities"
#| echo: false

architecture_criteria = pd.DataFrame({
    "Criterion": [
        "Risk Relevance",
        "Evidence Strength",
        "NIST Alignment",
        "Cost",
        "Feasibility",
        "Operational Impact",
        "Dependencies",
        "Time to Value",
    ],
    "Decision Meaning": [
        "Relevance to risk patterns identified in the breach analysis",
        "Strength of empirical and supporting evidence",
        "Consistency with applicable NIST guidance",
        "Relative implementation and operating burden",
        "Practicality of implementation",
        "Expected effect on organizational operations",
        "Reliance on prerequisite technologies or processes",
        "Relative speed at which useful capability can be established",
    ],
})

display(architecture_criteria.style.hide(axis="index"))
```

The criteria provide a structured comparison rather than a causal estimate of
control effectiveness. Scores represent decision-analysis judgments informed by
the empirical findings, NIST guidance, and implementation considerations.

## Architecture Scoring

Candidate capabilities are scored from 1 to 5 across eight decision criteria.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-architecture-scores
#| output: false
#| tbl-cap: "Component scores for candidate security-architecture capabilities"
#| echo: true

architecture_scores = pd.DataFrame({
    "Capability": [
        "Identity and Access Management / Zero-Trust Access",
        "Network and Workload Security",
        "Security Monitoring and Detection",
        "Third-Party Access and Risk Governance",
        "Incident Response and Recovery Resilience",
    ],
    "Risk Relevance": [5, 5, 5, 4, 3],
    "Evidence Strength": [4, 5, 5, 4, 3],
    "NIST Alignment": [5, 5, 5, 5, 4],
    "Cost": [3, 3, 4, 4, 3],
    "Feasibility": [4, 4, 4, 4, 3],
    "Operational Impact": [4, 3, 4, 4, 3],
    "Dependencies": [3, 3, 4, 4, 3],
    "Time to Value": [4, 4, 5, 4, 3],
})

display(architecture_scores)
```

## Equal-Weight Ranking

The initial comparison gives equal importance to all eight criteria. Each
capability's score is therefore the arithmetic mean of its component scores.

$$
S_i = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}s_{ik}
$$

where \(S_i\) is the overall score for capability \(i\), \(s_{ik}\) is its score
on criterion \(k\), and \(K=8\) is the number of criteria.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-equal-weight-ranking
#| output: false
#| tbl-cap: "Equal-weight ranking of candidate security-architecture capabilities"
#| echo: false

criteria = [
    "Risk Relevance",
    "Evidence Strength",
    "NIST Alignment",
    "Cost",
    "Feasibility",
    "Operational Impact",
    "Dependencies",
    "Time to Value",
]

equal_weight_ranking = (
    architecture_scores[["Capability"]]
    .assign(
        Score=architecture_scores[criteria].mean(axis=1)
    )
    .sort_values("Score", ascending=False)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

equal_weight_ranking.insert(
    0,
    "Rank",
    np.arange(1, len(equal_weight_ranking) + 1),
)

display(
    equal_weight_ranking.style
    .format({"Score": "{:.2f}"})
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

Security Monitoring and Detection receives the highest equal-weight score.

## Risk-Focused Sensitivity Analysis

This scenario places greater weight on risk relevance, evidence strength, and
NIST alignment while retaining the same component scores.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-risk-focused-weights
#| output: false
#| tbl-cap: "Criterion weights for the risk-focused sensitivity analysis"
#| echo: true

risk_focused_weights = {
    "Risk Relevance": 0.20,
    "Evidence Strength": 0.20,
    "NIST Alignment": 0.15,
    "Cost": 0.10,
    "Feasibility": 0.10,
    "Operational Impact": 0.10,
    "Dependencies": 0.05,
    "Time to Value": 0.10,
}

    "Criterion": risk_focused_weights.keys(),
    "Weight": risk_focused_weights.values(),
})

display(
    weight_table.style
    .format({"Weight": "{:.0%}"})
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

The weighted score for capability \(i\) is calculated as:

$$
S_i = \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k s_{ik}
$$

where \(w_k\) is the weight assigned to criterion \(k\), \(s_{ik}\) is the
component score, and the criterion weights sum to 1.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-risk-focused-ranking
#| output: false
#| tbl-cap: "Risk-focused ranking of candidate security-architecture capabilities"
#| echo: false

weights = pd.Series(risk_focused_weights)

risk_focused_ranking = (
    architecture_scores[["Capability"]]
    .assign(
        Score=architecture_scores[criteria]
        .mul(weights)
        .sum(axis=1)
    )
    .sort_values("Score", ascending=False)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

risk_focused_ranking.insert(
    0,
    "Rank",
    risk_focused_ranking["Score"]
    .rank(method="min", ascending=False)
    .astype(int),
)

display(
    risk_focused_ranking.style
    .format({"Score": "{:.2f}"})
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

Security Monitoring and Detection remains the highest-ranked capability.

# Financial Decision Analysis

## Financial Model

Financial outcomes are evaluated under explicit scenario assumptions. Because
the HHS data lack an organization-year denominator, annual breach frequency is
treated as an assumption rather than an estimate from the dataset.

The observed severe-breach proportion is used as the conditional probability
that a reported breach is severe.

### Annualized Loss Expectancy

Baseline annualized loss expectancy is calculated as:

$$
ALE = \lambda \times p_s \times L
$$

where:

- \(\lambda\) = assumed annual breach frequency,
- \(p_s\) = probability that a breach is severe, conditional on a breach, and
- \(L\) = assumed financial loss associated with a severe breach.

### Avoided Loss

Expected annual avoided loss is:

$$
AL = ALE \times r
$$

where \(r\) is the assumed proportional reduction in expected loss associated
with the investment.

### Annual Net Benefit

Annual net benefit is calculated as:

$$
NB = AL - C_o
$$

where \(C_o\) is annual operating cost.

### Net Present Value

For an initial investment \(C_0\), annual net benefit \(NB\), discount rate
\(d\), and investment horizon \(T\), net present value is:

$$
NPV =
-C_0
+
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
\frac{NB}{(1+d)^t}
$$

### Break-Even Risk Reduction

The minimum risk reduction required for the investment to achieve an NPV of
zero is:

$$
r_{BE}
=
\frac{
\frac{C_0}{PVAF(d,T)} + C_o
}{
ALE
}
$$

where the present-value annuity factor is:

$$
PVAF(d,T)
=
\frac{1-(1+d)^{-T}}{d}
$$

### Payback Period

When annual net benefit is positive, the simple payback period is:

$$
\text{Payback}
=
\frac{C_0}{NB}
$$

If annual net benefit is zero or negative, the investment does not have a
finite simple payback period under the evaluated assumptions.

## Financial Assumptions and Scenario Inputs

The observed severe-breach proportion is combined with scenario assumptions for
breach frequency, loss, investment cost, operating cost, and risk reduction.

The severe-breach probability is calculated directly from the HHS analytic
sample:

$$
p_s = \frac{801}{7{,}877} \approx 0.1017
$$

The remaining inputs are scenario assumptions used to evaluate financial
conditions rather than estimates produced by the HHS breach data.

## Primary Financial Scenario Analysis

The same financial model is applied to the Low, Expected, and High scenarios.

```{python}
#| label: financial-analysis-function
#| echo: true

def evaluate_investment(
    breach_frequency,
    severe_probability,
    loss_per_severe_breach,
    initial_cost,
    annual_operating_cost,
    risk_reduction,
    discount_rate=0.013,
    horizon=5,
):
    """Evaluate the financial performance of a security investment scenario."""

    baseline_ale = (
        breach_frequency
        * severe_probability
        * loss_per_severe_breach
    )

    avoided_loss = baseline_ale * risk_reduction
    annual_net_benefit = avoided_loss - annual_operating_cost

    pv_annuity_factor = sum(
        1 / (1 + discount_rate) ** year
        for year in range(1, horizon + 1)
    )

    npv = (
        -initial_cost
        + annual_net_benefit * pv_annuity_factor
    )

    break_even_risk_reduction = (
        initial_cost / pv_annuity_factor
        + annual_operating_cost
    ) / baseline_ale

    payback_years = (
        initial_cost / annual_net_benefit
        if annual_net_benefit > 0
        else np.nan
    )

    return {
        "Baseline ALE": baseline_ale,
        "Avoided Loss per Year": avoided_loss,
        "Annual Net Benefit": annual_net_benefit,
        "5-Year NPV": npv,
        "Break-Even Risk Reduction": break_even_risk_reduction,
        "Payback Years": payback_years,
    }
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-primary-financial-results
#| tbl-cap: "Primary financial scenario results"
#| echo: false

scenario_inputs = {
    "Low": {

        "initial_cost": 250_000,
        "annual_operating_cost": 100_000,

    },
    "Expected": {

        "annual_operating_cost": 400_000,
        "risk_reduction": 0.40,
    },
}

financial_results = []

for scenario, inputs in scenario_inputs.items():
    result = evaluate_investment(

        ),
```

None of the primary scenarios produces positive five-year NPV or finite simple

## Break-Even Risk Reduction Sensitivity

Required break-even risk reduction is evaluated across initial and recurring
cost combinations.

The Expected scenario baseline annualized loss expectancy is used as the
reference exposure:

$$
ALE =
0.235 \times p_s \times \$7.42\text{ million}
$$

For each cost combination, the break-even risk reduction is calculated as:

$$
r_{BE}
=
\frac{
\frac{C_0}{PVAF(d,T)} + C_o
}{
ALE
}
$$

```{python}
#| label: tbl-break-even-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "Break-even risk reduction by initial investment and annual operating cost"
#| echo: false

initial_costs = [
    100_000,
    250_000,
    500_000,
    750_000,
    1_000_000,
]

annual_operating_costs = [
    0,
    25_000,
    50_000,
    100_000,
    200_000,
]

expected_ale = (
    0.235
    * severe_probability
    * 7_420_000
)

discount_rate = 0.013
horizon = 5

pv_annuity_factor = sum(
    1 / (1 + discount_rate) ** year
    for year in range(1, horizon + 1)
)

break_even_results = []

for initial_cost in initial_costs:
    row = {
        "Initial Investment Cost": initial_cost,
    }

    for annual_cost in annual_operating_costs:
        break_even_rate = (
            initial_cost / pv_annuity_factor
            + annual_cost
        ) / expected_ale

        row[f"${annual_cost:,.0f}"] = break_even_rate * 100

    break_even_results.append(row)

break_even_sensitivity = pd.DataFrame(
    break_even_results
)

display(
    break_even_sensitivity.style
    .format({
        "Initial Investment Cost": "${:,.0f}",
        "$0": "{:.1f}%",
        "$25,000": "{:.1f}%",
        "$50,000": "{:.1f}%",
        "$100,000": "{:.1f}%",
        "$200,000": "{:.1f}%",
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

Required risk reduction increases with both initial and recurring cost.

## Risk-Assumption Sensitivity

Five-year NPV is evaluated across annual breach-frequency and severe-loss
assumptions while holding the remaining inputs constant.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-risk-assumption-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "Five-year NPV sensitivity to annual breach frequency and loss per severe breach"
#| echo: false

breach_frequencies = [
    0.14,
    0.235,
    0.33,
]

loss_assumptions = [
    5_000_000,
    7_420_000,
    10_000_000,
]

risk_sensitivity_results = []

for breach_frequency in breach_frequencies:
    row = {
        "Annual Breach Frequency": breach_frequency,
    }

    for loss_value in loss_assumptions:
        result = evaluate_investment(
            breach_frequency=breach_frequency,
            severe_probability=severe_probability,
            loss_per_severe_breach=loss_value,
            initial_cost=250_000,
            annual_operating_cost=50_000,
            risk_reduction=0.30,
            discount_rate=0.013,
            horizon=5,
        )

        row[f"${loss_value:,.0f}"] = result["5-Year NPV"]

    risk_sensitivity_results.append(row)

risk_sensitivity = pd.DataFrame(
    risk_sensitivity_results
)

display(
    risk_sensitivity.style
    .format({
        "Annual Breach Frequency": "{:.3f}",
        "$5,000,000": "${:,.0f}",
        "$7,420,000": "${:,.0f}",
        "$10,000,000": "${:,.0f}",
    })
    .hide(axis="index")
)
```

Higher assumed breach frequency and severe-breach loss improve NPV, but no
tested combination produces positive five-year NPV.

# Limitations and Interpretation Boundaries

This analysis uses publicly reported breach records and therefore reflects the
scope, definitions, and reporting practices of the source system. The data do
not represent the complete population of security incidents, and changes in
reporting practices may contribute to observed temporal patterns.

The regression estimates adjusted associations rather than causal effects or
organization-specific breach probabilities. Cluster assignments are
exploratory summaries of recurring feature combinations and are not treated as
independent predictors in the primary regression. The architecture rankings
depend on explicitly documented scoring assumptions, while the financial
results are scenarios rather than realized organizational returns.

```{python}
for filename, table in export_tables.items():

    export_table.to_csv(
        output_path,
        index=preserve_index,
        encoding="utf-8",
    )

    manifest_records.append({
        "File": filename,
        "Rows": export_table.shape[0],
        "Columns": export_table.shape[1],
        "Index Exported": preserve_index,
        "Size (KB)": round(output_path.stat().st_size / 1024, 2),
    })

export_manifest = pd.DataFrame(manifest_records)
manifest_path = output_dir / "analysis_output_manifest.csv"
export_manifest.to_csv(manifest_path, index=False, encoding="utf-8")

workbook_path = output_dir / "HHS_HIPAA_analysis_results.xlsx"
used_sheet_names = set()

with pd.ExcelWriter(workbook_path, engine="openpyxl") as writer:
    for filename, table in export_tables.items():
        base_name = Path(filename).stem.replace("_", " ")[:31]
        sheet_name = base_name
        suffix = 1

        while sheet_name in used_sheet_names:
            suffix += 1
            sheet_name = f"{base_name[:27]} {suffix}"

        used_sheet_names.add(sheet_name)
        preserve_index = not isinstance(table.index, pd.RangeIndex)

        table.to_excel(
            writer,
            sheet_name=sheet_name,
            index=preserve_index,
        )

        worksheet = writer.sheets[sheet_name]
        worksheet.freeze_panes = "A2"
        worksheet.auto_filter.ref = worksheet.dimensions

        for column_cells in worksheet.columns:
            values = [
                str(cell.value)
                for cell in column_cells
                if cell.value is not None
            ]
            maximum_width = max(
                (len(value) for value in values),
                default=10,
            )
            worksheet.column_dimensions[
                column_cells[0].column_letter
            ].width = min(max(maximum_width + 2, 12), 45)

environment_information = {

with environment_path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    json.dump(environment_information, file, indent=2)

archive_path = output_dir / "HHS_HIPAA_analysis_outputs.zip"
with zipfile.ZipFile(

print(f"Exported {len(export_tables)} analysis tables.")
```
